pass_a_gloss: (the life unto) incorruption, being transformed in blessedness and sanctification to the condition at the beginning, and as it were going backward, being conformed to the age to come. What then is the sacrifice befitting the new moons, that is, the one in Christ and spiritual, and also the life according to the age to come? The dying to God, and living no longer held by sins, but departing altogether from the more earthy citizenship, so that we may live together with Christ. So also the divine Paul writes to those sanctified in the Spirit and justified in Christ and instructed in the powers of the age to come, saying: 'If you died in Christ, why as living in the world do you subject yourselves to decrees?' And again: 'For you died, and your life has been hidden with Christ in God. When Christ our life is manifested, then you too will be manifested with him in glory.' See then how in differing quantity of spiritual good condition those accustomed to be well approved die sacredly to God, and at once gain the prizes of goodness. For calves are sacrificed, two, and one ram with them, and seven lambs, not having a blemish. And through all these the multitude of the saints is inscribed for us, as excelling in the highest virtue, through the calves, and sinking down as it were also in second things, as in the ram, and in the lesser and lower again in the lambs. Two then are the calves; for two are the peoples; and one ram in between, on account of the union of the two into oneness in Christ. And seven again lambs; for in the most perfect fullness is the populace of the saints. And being two, and one according to the spiritual union, the multitude would reasonably be understood as most perfect. For very broad, both in the simplicity in Christ and in the infancy according to him, is the herd of the believers. And observe how three tenths of fine flour for the one calf is the portion set apart, and in half of the hin, that is, six pints (xestai), both oil and wine. And for the ram, two tenths of fine flour, and in a third of the hin the things poured on. And for each of the lambs one tenth of fine flour the sacrifice, and in a fourth of the hin the libation, that is, both oil and wine. For of equal weight to the toils of each, and also to the powers according to virtue, the measure of the life, the one as in renown and blessedness I say, and also of union from God, and of spiritual gladness, will be allotted by the one judging the just things; for have we not very many times said that the fine flour fills up the type of life, and the oil of richness, and the wine of the spiritual gladness? PALL.: Very much so. CYR.: And a he-goat again is added to the sacrifices, slaughtered on behalf of sins, for a type of Christ. For acceptable is our sacrifice and pleasing to God through the saving passion of Christ. And this, I think, is what the Savior himself said to the holy apostles: 'Apart from me you can do nothing.' So necessarily to our fragrances Christ's is added, in a certain way mixing itself up with ours, and taking them up together to the Fa(ther) (continues).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …incorruptible life, as we are transformed in blessedness and holiness back to what was at the beginning, and, going backward as it were, are conformed to the age to come. What, then, is the sacrifice that befits the new moons, that is, the spiritual new moon in Christ, and the life of the age to come? To die to God, and no longer to live held fast by sins, but to depart altogether from the more earthly way of life, so that we may live with Christ. So too the inspired Paul writes to those sanctified in the Spirit, justified in Christ, and taught the powers of the age to come, saying, ‘If you died in Christ, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to decrees?’ (Colossians 2:20). And again: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory’ (Colossians 3:3–4).

See, then, how those who are used to being well approved die sacredly to God in differing measures of spiritual vigor, and at once win the rewards of goodness. For two calves are sacrificed, and one ram with them, and seven lambs without blemish. Through all these the multitude of the saints is described for us: as excelling in the highest virtue, through the calves; as sitting a little lower, in the second rank as it were, as in the ram; and again as in the lesser and humbler virtue, in the lambs. The calves are two, for the peoples are two; and one ram between them, because of the union of the two into one in Christ. The lambs, again, are seven, for the people of the saints is in the most perfect fullness. And since they are two, and yet one by spiritual union, the multitude may fittingly be understood as most perfect. For the flock of those who believe is very broad, both in the simplicity that is in Christ and in the childlikeness that is after his pattern.

Notice how three tenths of fine flour are set apart for the one calf, and oil and wine in half a hin, that is, six pints. For the ram, two tenths of fine flour, and what is poured on in a third of a hin. For each of the lambs, one tenth of fine flour is the sacrifice, and a quarter of a hin is the drink offering, that is, oil and wine. For in equal weight with each one’s labors, and with his powers in virtue, the measure of life will be allotted by the one who judges justly: of life in renown and blessedness, I mean, and of union with God, and of spiritual gladness. Have we not said very often that the fine flour serves as a type of life, the oil of richness, and the wine of spiritual gladness?

Cyril: A male goat, again, is added to the sacrifices, slaughtered for sins, as a type of Christ. For our sacrifice is acceptable and pleasing to God because of the saving passion of Christ. And this, I think, is what the Savior himself said to the holy apostles: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5). So Christ’s fragrance is of necessity added to our fragrances, blending itself in a way with ours and carrying them up with it to the Father…

choices.why: Dative kept: death offered to God as sacrifice; Cyril then says the saints 'die sacredly to God'.
